patient.chief_complaint: Two episodes of right-sided limb weakness with left occipital headache over the past 3 weeks — sent for urgent evaluation
patient.hpi:
A 39-year-old Japanese man with a long-standing history of myofascial pain syndrome and intermittent headaches was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic for urgent evaluation after two episodes of transient right-sided limb weakness. The first episode occurred 20 days prior to this visit: he noticed weakness in his right arm and right leg while at home, along with a tense, numb feeling on the right side of his face. These symptoms developed gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes and resolved over the following 30-40 minutes. Afterwards, he experienced a left occipital headache that he treated with loxoprofen with good relief.

The second episode occurred 2 days before this visit. He was at work when he again developed right upper and lower limb weakness and a tense feeling on the left side of his mouth. He was found unresponsive by a colleague and transported by ambulance to a local emergency department. En route to hospital, he regained consciousness and complained of a left occipital headache. At the emergency department, he was alert with right limb weakness and sensory disturbance over the ulnar aspect of the right upper arm. He was admitted for observation. His symptoms gradually improved over several hours and he was discharged with an outpatient referral when no acute cause was identified.

He has a history of migraine headaches and myofascial pain, managed with lomerizine hydrochloride and as-needed NSAIDs. He has no prior stroke, no hypertension, no diabetes, and no cardiac disease. He is a non-smoker. He reports no family history of hemiplegic migraine. He is now headache-free and fully neurologically intact at this consultation.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Sporadic hemiplegic migraine (G43.1) — two qualifying episodes with gradual motor and sensory aura followed by headache; all secondary causes excluded

critical_actions: Brain MRI with DWI to exclude acute infarction — TIA/stroke is the primary differential given acute hemiplegia
EEG to exclude epilepsy with Todd's paralysis — brief loss of consciousness at second episode
Serum and CSF lactate to exclude MELAS — episodic neurological episodes with headache
Gradual onset over 20-25 minutes is the KEY feature distinguishing CSD (sporadic hemiplegic migraine) from embolic TIA (sudden maximal onset)
Avoid triptans during motor aura episodes
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe triptans during motor aura episodes (cautioned in hemiplegic migraine)
Do not diagnose TIA without DWI restriction — normal DWI is reassuring; gradual onset argues against TIA
Do not close PFO without confirmed stroke — no PFO found on this workup
key_reasoning_points: Gradual progression of motor weakness over 20-25 minutes = cortical spreading depression propagation rate (3-5 mm/min) — characteristic of hemiplegic migraine aura, not embolic TIA
ICHD-3 sporadic hemiplegic migraine requires ≥2 qualifying motor aura attacks and no first/second degree relative with identical attacks — criteria met
The second episode's transient loss of consciousness can occur in severe hemiplegic migraine — not required to change diagnosis to epilepsy without EEG evidence
MELAS shares clinical features (episodic neurological deficits, headache) but is distinguished by elevated lactate, mitochondrial DNA mutation, and maternal inheritance — all normal/negative here

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Sporadic Hemiplegic Migraine — ICHD-3 Criteria and TIA Differentiation

ICHD-3 CRITERIA FOR SPORADIC HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE (SHM):
1. Migraine with motor aura: ≥2 attacks with fully reversible motor weakness as one aura symptom
2. ≥1 other aura symptom (visual, sensory, or language) spreading gradually
3. No first- or second-degree relative with identical attacks (distinguishes from familial hemiplegic migraine)
4. Normal neuroimaging and no other explanation

TIA VS HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE AURA:
  TIA: Sudden onset, maximal at onset; motor weakness abrupt; typically brief; not consistently followed by headache
  HM aura: Gradual progression over ≥5 min; motor weakness accompanies other aura features; typically followed by headache within 60 min

KEY DIFFERENTIATING FEATURES:
  Cortical spreading depression propagation speed approximately 3-5 mm/min — produces gradual symptom onset over 20+ minutes
  Embolic/ischaemic TIA is maximal at onset
  Prior migraine history and gradual spread are key clinical features

Clinical correlation recommended.
output.summary: ICHD-3 SHM requires ≥2 reversible motor aura attacks, gradual onset of aura over ≥5 min, and no first/second-degree relative with identical attacks; gradual motor spread distinguishes from embolic TIA

output.report:
DRUG REVIEW — TRIPTANS IN HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE

FINDINGS: Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) exert vasoconstrictive effects on cerebral and meningeal vasculature. In the context of hemiplegic migraine — where motor aura is associated with cortical spreading depression and haemodynamic changes — most international guidelines caution against triptan use during motor aura episodes due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk, although the evidence base is limited.

CATEGORY: Triptans are cautioned (not universally absolutely contraindicated) in hemiplegic migraine; individual guideline recommendations vary. Clinical correlation recommended.
output.summary: Triptans are cautioned in hemiplegic migraine due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk during motor aura; category-level caution applies; clinical correlation required
